name: Scroll-Video Scrub
summary: A section pins in the viewport and scroll position becomes the playhead: scrolling scrubs a video/frame-sequence forward frame-by-frame instead of moving the page. The visitor controls the cinematic reveal's speed, making a linear film feel interactive.

composition: The opening frame is a composed poster (subject + giant name + copy corners) that deliberately DISASSEMBLES as the scrub advances — type clears, camera pushes in, and the sequence resolves on a tight subject close-up.
A scroll-progress indicator is required: the visitor must know they are inside a pinned sequence and how much remains.
A vertical side label or eyebrow keeps a magazine frame around the footage.
layering: Scrubbed footage is the full-bleed base plane → a colored gradient wash/scrim → overlay type and UI on top.
Depth comes from the camera move INSIDE the footage (push-in, dolly), not from stacked layers — the film provides the parallax.
Overlay elements bind to scrub progress, entering and exiting at authored timeline positions.
lighting: Light is the footage's cinematography (stage/concert/location lighting); a colored gradient scrim can unify and brand it.
The brightest element should be the type accent so the frame keeps a focal hierarchy while footage changes under it.
typography: Ultra-bold condensed display for the anchor word/name; it rides the scrub timeline — fading out early to hand the frame to the subject.
Small script or eyebrow accents tie entrances to specific playhead positions.

rules: A single gradient wash over the footage + one loud complementary accent for type/CTA creates maximum energy with two decisions.
The accent must survive every frame of the sequence — test it against the brightest and darkest frames.

easing: The footage itself is LINEAR with scroll — no independent easing; smoothing belongs in a small scroll-position damper, not the mapping.
Overlay type uses quick fades/slides at its timeline marks.
pacing: The visitor sets the pace; the design decision is the scroll-distance-to-frames ratio — long enough to feel cinematic, short enough not to trap.
The pin releases crisply at sequence end; trapping scroll past the payoff kills trust.
choreography: Scroll leads everything: progress → camera push → type exits → subject resolve; a progress marker tracks the sequence.
Text choreography is authored against the playhead (enter at 10%, exit by 40%), never against wall-clock time.

gapNotes: The scroll-scrub driver exists (W8: section-scrub + global scroll binding) but there is no frame-sequence/video-texture asset type to scrub — the R2 pre-rendered sequence pipeline is exactly the W-PHOTO deliverable.
Pinned-section behavior (section holds while scroll drives an internal timeline) is unproven in the prism runtime's preview scroll model.
No source for footage: needs either user upload or a pre-rendered sequence generated from our own 3D scenes (render-to-frames path, W-PHOTO).

whenToUse: Artist/performer/venue intros, product reveals, and any hero whose story is a single camera move.
When the brief wants 'interactive film' — the visitor drives, so it reads as craft rather than autoplay.
whenNotToUse: Fast-utility or content-first sites: the pin delays access to everything below.
Mobile-heavy audiences on constrained bandwidth — frame sequences are heavy; must degrade to a static poster + normal scroll.
Briefs with no real footage or renderable scene — the family cannot fake its core asset.

notes: The scrub owns the scroll axis — never combine with a second scroll-hijacking family on the same page.
Kinetic type pairs well because both bind to the same playhead.

antiRepetition.notes: Same cluster as cinematic-video-hero and media-showreel-gallery.

sources.title: DJ Website Template with Scroll Video
sources.motionEvidence: Founder monitor session, live demo: hero pinned and scrubbed via scroll through full progress in both directions; camera push-in, early name fade-out, and the bottom progress indicator all observed tracking the playhead.
